nameStory: The rufous-backed cellophane bee gets its name from two distinctive features: the rusty-red (rufous) coloring on its back and thorax, and the cellophane-like material it uses to line its nest cells. This 'cellophane' is actually a waterproof, transparent secretion that the female bee produces to protect her eggs and food stores from moisture.
description: The rufous-backed cellophane bee is a solitary ground-nesting bee with distinctive rusty-red coloring on its back and chest areas. These medium-sized native bees are about half an inch long and have a somewhat fuzzy appearance with darker wings. Unlike honeybees that live in colonies, each female digs her own burrow in sandy soil where she creates waterproof cells for her eggs. They're important native pollinators that emerge in late summer and fall when many other bees are less active.

idTips.label: Rufous coloring
idTips.description: Look for distinctive rusty-red to orange-brown hair covering the thorax (middle section) and often extending onto the abdomen, giving it a warm, coppery appearance in sunlight

idTips.label: Ground nesting behavior
idTips.description: Watch for bees flying low over sandy areas and disappearing into small holes in the ground, often creating little piles of excavated soil around nest entrances

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Notice their somewhat heavy, deliberate flight style as they move between flowers and nesting sites, less zippy than smaller sweat bees

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About the size of a small honeybee (roughly half an inch) but with a more robust, fuzzy appearance and relatively large head compared to body size

idTips.label: Wing appearance
idTips.description: Wings have a slightly smoky or amber tint and make a distinctive low buzzing sound, different from the higher pitch of smaller bees

habitat: Look for rufous-backed cellophane bees in areas with sandy, well-drained soil where they can easily excavate their nests, such as coastal dunes, sandy river banks, and disturbed areas with loose soil. They prefer open sunny locations near their preferred flowers, often found in coastal plain habitats and sandy openings in pine barrens. The females need both suitable nesting soil and access to late-season flowers for foraging.

seasonality.spring: Not active during spring months. Larvae are developing underground in their waterproof cells, slowly growing on stored pollen provisions left by their mothers.
seasonality.summer: Early to mid-summer sees continued larval development underground. By late summer, watch for newly emerged adults beginning to appear and search for mates.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity occurs in fall when adults are most visible, actively foraging on late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod, and females are busy excavating nests and provisioning cells.
seasonality.winter: Adults die after the first hard frosts, leaving behind eggs or young larvae safely sealed in underground waterproof cells that will survive winter freezing.

funFact: Female rufous-backed cellophane bees are like tiny chemists, secreting a natural polyester-like substance from their abdomens that they paint onto their nest walls with their tongues - this 'cellophane' is so effective that scientists have studied it for potential applications in waterproof packaging!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cellophane bees in the same genus, but the rufous-backed is one of the few with such prominent rusty-red coloring on the thorax. Remember: 'Rufous on the back, you're on the right track' - if you see that distinctive coppery-red fuzzy chest area, you've likely found your species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'cellophane bee' can be confusing since it has nothing to do with the man-made cellophane wrap - these bees were actually producing their transparent waterproof nest linings millions of years before humans invented plastic packaging. The family name 'plasterer bees' comes from their behavior of 'plastering' their nest walls with this natural secretion.
compareHints: Among New England's cellophane bees, the rufous-backed stands out for its prominent rusty-red thoracic hair, while most relatives like the unequal cellophane bee have more subdued brown or gray coloring. The blueberry cellophane bee is active much earlier in the year (spring), and the aster cellophane bee, while also fall-active, typically has less distinct rufous coloring and prefers different flower types.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Unequal Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its preference for early spring tree blossoms, especially maples and willows, while relatives like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee specialize in late-season flowers.
Among New England's cellophane bees, the Spine-shouldered stands out primarily due to its namesake shoulder spines, which most relatives lack.

Unlike the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee which specializes on late-summer flowers, or the Aster Cellophane Bee found on fall composites, the Blueberry Cellophane Bee is strictly a spring specialist of heath family plants.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the Aster Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its late-season activity and aster specialization, while the Unequal Cellophane Bee flies much earlier in spring when fruit trees bloom.

Among New England's dozen cellophane bee species, the Broad-footed stands out with its notably wide tarsi, while species like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee or Aster Cellophane Bee are named for their flower preferences rather than physical features.
